signals.brief_en:
Title: Larissa-Caitlin/paypal-hackathon-agent-firewall
Brief: A payment firewall prototype designed to block prompt‑injected AI shopping agents from misdirecting payments. The system integrates a PayPal sandbox with LLM‑based validation checks that verify merchant identifiers before authorising a transaction. Early tests show it can intercept malformed prompts, but coverage against sophisticated prompt‑injection techniques remains uncertain.

signals.title: @noxflux: GOOGLE EYES DATA SECURITY ROLE IN PENTAGON GOLDEN DOME PROGRAM Alphabet unit Google is in early talks with the Pentagon about helping secure
signals.content: GOOGLE EYES DATA SECURITY ROLE IN PENTAGON GOLDEN DOME PROGRAM Alphabet unit Google is in early talks with the Pentagon about helping secure the data behind the $185B Golden Dome missile defense program, according to Bloomberg. The Defense Department is setting up an industry consortium to protect the data pipelines that feed the program's core command-and-control software. The talks focus on Google's data storage, networking and cybersecurity tools. The aim is to keep military communications running even if adversaries knock out ground networks or cell towers. Aalyria Technologies, a networking company spun out of Google, is also involved in the consortium. Google and Aalyria declined to comment. Nothing is final yet. A Pentagon official said the department is still weighing early concepts and has not decided the consortium's structure or which companies will take part. The move continues Google's shift back toward defense work. The company left the Pentagon's Project Maven in 2018 after employee protests. In April 2026 it signed a deal allowing its AI models to be used for classified military work. $GOOGL

signals.brief_en:
Title: sudosubin/agents.nix
Source: Nixpkgs overlay that aggregates AI agent skill definitions from the public repositories skills.sh and skillsdirectory.com. The overlay provides a declarative, reproducible way to import, version‑pin, and configure these skill modules within Nix environments. It enables rapid composition of agent capabilities while preserving provenance and allowing OSINT analysts to verify the origin and version of each skill set. Uncertainty remains regarding the completeness of the skill catalog and any licensing constraints of the upstream sources.

signals.title: mdussere/tanstaafllm
signals.content: A personal project to give a 1-GB Linux handheld an AI-native life, built by a cell of coding agents under human control. Told as a nod to Heinlein's The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress: the agents play the lunar rebels, and the cause is "There Ain't No Such Thing As A Free LLM": least sufficient intelligence, visible costs, no bloat.
signals.score_reason: high-value open-source ecosystem signal; agentic AI relevance; large language model relevance. Final score: 68. Freshness: source age 0d.
signals.brief_en: Project 'mdussere/tanstaafllm' explores deploying an AI-native OS environment on a 1-GB Linux handheld device using human-directed coding agents. Inspired by Heinlein's 'The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress', the effort focuses on the principle 'There Ain't No Such Thing As A Free LLM' (TANSTAAFFLLM), prioritizing least-sufficient intelligence, strict resource constraints, low latency, and operational cost transparency over bloated architectures.

signals.title: @OpenAI: Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s at
signals.content: Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training. Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action. To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review. To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident. In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway. As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene. https://t.co/dIYP7B1GlD
